turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Hi there, I'm Dr. Quamer -Sant,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: one of the dermatologists here.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Did you find parking okay?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That garage is a maze.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Ah, it really is. I went around twice before I found a spot on level three. Everybody does.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: So before we start, can you tell me your full name and date of birth?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Aisling Brennan, and my birthday is June 9th, 1988.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Thank you, Aisling. Your referral mentions a mole on your back. Tell me what's going on with it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So it's on my left upper back, kind of by my shoulder blade. My husband Declan noticed it looked different back in um July. He says it's gotten bigger and darker since spring. Okay, has it bled at all or crusted over? No, no bleeding.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Does it itch or hurt?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It itches a little now and then, it doesn't hurt.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Have you ever had a skin cancer yourself self, or any moles removed.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I've never had skin cancer,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: and nothing's ever been removed. Anyone in the family with skin cancer.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My dad had a basal cell on his nose a few years ago. They scraped it off and he's been fine. Good to know.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: How about sun exposure?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sunburns growing up tanning beds. Oh, lots of sun. I was a lifeguard every summer through college at Crestview Aquatics. I got burned pretty badly a few times, like blistering. Never did tanning beds, though. Got it.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Any medicines you take regularly.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Just Levotheric sign. Seventy -five micrograms every morning for my thyroid.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: And any allergies to medications? Or to lidocaine or latex? No allergies that I know of. All right, let me take a look.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Can you slip your left arm out of the gown? Okay.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: So on your left upper back, just over the shoulder blade, there's a seven millimeter dark brown mole. It's asymmetric, the border is irregular and kind of gnarched at the bottom, and there's a black area on one side. Under the dermatar scope, I see an irregular network and a few darts at the edge. That one stands out from your other moles.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Is that bad?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: It's what we call an ugly duckling, it doesn't look like its neighbours. Let me check the rest of you first. Your back, chest and arms have scattered two to three millimetre round moles, evenly brown. on. Those all look like normal benign moles. Scalp, face and legs look fine. I don't feel any swollen lymph nodes in your left armpit or your neck, any lumps you've noticed in your armpit.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Okay, so here's what I think. This mole on your back has several changing features. Most of these turn out to be an atypical mole, but I can't rule out an early melanoma just by looking. So today, okay, what does that involve?" It's a shave biopsy.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I numbed the area with a little lidocaine with epinephrine,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: then I take off the whole mole with a thin blade, fairly deep,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: and send it to the lab.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: No stitches.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: You'll have a shallow wound,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: kind of like a scrape.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's fine, let's do it.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Great, a little pinch and a burn now. Okay, and that's done, it went well. I've sent it to pathology. For care, keep the bandage on for twenty -four hours, then wash it gently once a day, put on plain petroleum jelly and a fresh bandage every day until it heals. That's usually one to two weeks.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, when will I know?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Results take about seven to ten days. They'll post to the portal, and someone will call you either way. What's the best number for you? My cell, 555 -0163, and my portal email is ashlingdartbrennan88 at fastmail .com.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Got it. If it does come back as a melanoma,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: we'd talk about a wider excision to get clear margins, but let's not get ahead of ourselves. If the sight gets red,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: heart,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: swollen or drains pus, call us. Okay, should I be doing anything about the sun? Yes, broad -spectrum sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, every day on exposed skin, reapply every two hours when you're outside, and a wide -brimmed hat. Check your own moles once a month. And since you've had blistering sunburns and quite a few moles, I'd like to see you for a full skin check every year.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sounds good.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Let's book a follow -up for the biopsy site and results on Tuesday, October 27th.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Any other questions. No, I think that's it. Thank you. You're welcome,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Aisling.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Take care and good luck getting out of that garage.
